topics.title: Callbacks and the Error-First Pattern
topics.summary: The original async style in Node: pass a function that receives (err, result), and avoid callback hell.
topics.description:
Early Node did all asynchronous work with **callbacks**: a function you pass in that Node calls later when the operation finishes.

### The error-first convention
Node callbacks always take the error as the **first** argument and the result second:

`fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { if (err) return handle(err); use(data); })`

If `err` is `null` or `undefined` the operation succeeded. Always check it first and `return` so you do not continue.

### Rules of good callback APIs
1. The callback is called **once**
2. The callback is called **either always sync or always async** (never mixed; "releasing Zalgo")
3. Errors are never thrown, they are passed to the callback

### Callback hell
Dependent steps nest deeper and deeper: read a file, parse it, query a database, write a result. The code drifts to the right, error handling is repeated at each level and it is easy to forget a `return`.

### Escape routes
* Name your functions and keep them flat
* Wrap callbacks with `util.promisify` and use `async/await`
* Use the promise versions of core modules (`fs/promises`)

### A try/catch trap
`try { fs.readFile(p, cb) } catch (e) {}` **does not catch** errors that happen later inside the async operation. The stack is gone by the time the callback runs.

### Where you still see them
Event emitters, older libraries, `process.nextTick`, `setTimeout`, and Express middleware `next(err)`.
keyPoints: Error-first: callback(err, result)
Check err first and return early
try/catch cannot catch errors from a later callback
Flatten nested callbacks or promisify them
pitfalls: Calling the callback twice (e.g. forgetting return after an error)
Throwing inside a callback, which crashes the process
Mixing sync and async invocation of the same callback

examples.explanation: The second version has one error handler and reads top to bottom.

interview.q: What is the error-first callback convention?
interview.a: The first argument of a callback is reserved for an error (null on success) and the following arguments carry the results, so callers can consistently check if (err) before using data.

interview.q: Why does try/catch not catch errors from async callbacks?
interview.a: The callback runs later from the event loop when the original call stack has already finished, so the try block is no longer active. Errors must be passed to the callback or handled with promises and await.

topics.title: Promises in Node
topics.summary: Promises represent a future value, can be chained and combined with Promise.all, allSettled, race and any.
topics.description:
A **Promise** is an object for a value that will exist later. It has three states: *pending*, *fulfilled* (with a value) or *rejected* (with an error). Once settled it never changes.

### Using promises
`fetchUser(1).then(user => user.name).catch(err => ...).finally(() => ...)`. Each `.then` returns a **new** promise, so you can chain. Returning a value passes it on; returning a promise waits for it; throwing becomes a rejection.

### Creating promises
`new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })` wraps callback APIs. Call `resolve` or `reject` exactly once. Most of the time you can use `util.promisify` or the built-in promise APIs instead of writing this by hand.

### Combinators
| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| `Promise.all([...])` | All values; rejects at the first failure |
| `Promise.allSettled([...])` | Waits for all; gives `{status, value/reason}` for each |
| `Promise.race([...])` | First to settle (value or error) |
| `Promise.any([...])` | First to **fulfil**; rejects only if all fail |
| `Promise.withResolvers()` | `{ promise, resolve, reject }` handy for events |

### Parallel vs sequential
Starting promises first and awaiting later runs them in parallel: `await Promise.all([a(), b()])`. Awaiting one after another runs them in sequence and takes the sum of both durations.

### Unhandled rejections
A rejected promise with no handler triggers `unhandledRejection`. Since Node 15 this **crashes the process** by default.

### Microtasks
`.then` callbacks run as microtasks, after the current synchronous code and before timers.

then/catch/finally return new promises, so they chain
Promise.all for parallel work, allSettled for tolerant collection
Unhandled rejections terminate modern Node by default
Create promises manually only when wrapping callback APIs
pitfalls: Forgetting to return a promise inside then (breaks the chain)

interview.q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled?
interview.a: all rejects as soon as any promise rejects and returns only values on success. allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome, so one failure does not hide the other results.

interview.q: What happens with an unhandled promise rejection in modern Node?
interview.a: Node emits unhandledRejection and, by default since v15, terminates the process with an error. Attach catch handlers or use try/catch with await.

topics.title: async/await and Concurrency Patterns
topics.summary: Write asynchronous code that reads like synchronous code, and control parallelism, retries and timeouts.
topics.description:
`async` functions always return a promise. Inside them, `await` pauses **that function** (not the whole program) until the promise settles. The event loop keeps serving other work in the meantime.

### Error handling
Use `try/catch/finally` around awaits. A rejected promise throws at the `await` line.

### Sequential vs parallel
Slow: `const a = await getA(); const b = await getB();` (sum of times).
Fast: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);` (the longer of the two).

### await in loops
`for (const id of ids) await load(id)` is **sequential**. `forEach(async ...)` does not wait at all. For parallel use `Promise.all(ids.map(load))`. For huge lists limit concurrency (batches, `p-limit`, or a small queue) so you do not open thousands of connections at once.

### Top-level await
Available in ES modules, so scripts can `await` directly without wrapping in `main()`.

### Common patterns
* **Timeout**: `Promise.race([work(), rejectAfter(ms)])`, better with `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`
* **Retry with backoff**: loop with `await sleep(2 ** attempt * 100)`
* **Async iteration**: `for await (const chunk of stream)`
* **Fire and forget**: call without await but always attach `.catch(log)`

### Return await
Inside `try/catch` use `return await fn()`; without `await` a rejection escapes your catch.

Use Promise.all for independent work; await sequentially only for dependent steps
forEach does not await its async callbacks
Limit concurrency for large batches
Use return await inside try/catch

interview.q: Why is array.forEach(async ...) a bug?
interview.a: forEach ignores the promises returned by the callback, so code after it runs before the async work completes and errors become unhandled. Use for...of with await, or Promise.all with map.

interview.q: How do you limit concurrency?
interview.a: Process items in chunks with Promise.all, use a semaphore/queue, or a library such as p-limit or p-queue, so only N operations run at once.

topics.title: The Event Loop in Depth
topics.summary: The six libuv phases (timers, pending, idle/prepare, poll, check, close) and how Node decides what to run next.
topics.description:
The **event loop** is what lets one thread handle thousands of concurrent tasks. After your main script finishes, Node enters the loop and keeps cycling through **phases**. Each phase has a queue of callbacks.

### The phases in order
1. **timers**: runs expired `setTimeout` / `setInterval` callbacks
2. **pending callbacks**: some deferred system callbacks (e.g. certain TCP errors)
3. **idle, prepare**: internal use
4. **poll**: retrieves new I/O events and runs their callbacks (file reads, sockets, HTTP). If nothing is queued it may **wait here** for I/O (but not past the next timer, and not if `setImmediate` callbacks are waiting)
5. **check**: runs `setImmediate` callbacks
6. **close callbacks**: e.g. `socket.on('close')`

Between **every callback** (since Node 11), Node drains the `process.nextTick` queue and then the promise microtask queue.

### Who does the real work?
* Network I/O uses the OS (epoll, kqueue, IOCP): no extra threads
* File system, DNS lookup, crypto, zlib use the **libuv thread pool** (4 threads by default, `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` up to 1024)
* Results are delivered back to the loop as callbacks

### The loop ends when nothing is left
No pending timers, handles, requests or servers: the process exits. An open server or `setInterval` keeps it alive.

### Blocking the loop
Any long synchronous work in a callback delays **everything**: timers fire late, requests stall. Typical culprits: large `JSON.parse`, regex catastrophes, sync fs/crypto, big loops.

### Quick intuition
timers → poll (I/O) → check (setImmediate) → close, repeated forever, with microtasks drained after each callback.
keyPoints: Phases: timers, pending, idle/prepare, poll, check, close
nextTick and promise microtasks run between callbacks
Network I/O is OS-driven; files, DNS, crypto, zlib use the 4-thread pool
Long synchronous code blocks every phase
The process exits when no work remains
pitfalls: Assuming the thread pool handles network sockets
Running CPU-heavy work in a callback and freezing the loop
Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs immediately

interview.q: Explain the phases of the Node.js event loop.
interview.a: timers (setTimeout/setInterval), pending callbacks, idle/prepare, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate) and close callbacks. After each callback, Node drains process.nextTick and then promise microtasks. The loop repeats until there is nothing left to do.

interview.q: What uses the libuv thread pool?
interview.a: fs operations, dns.lookup, crypto functions such as pbkdf2/scrypt/randomBytes, and zlib. Sockets and most network I/O use the operating system's non-blocking mechanisms instead.

topics.title: nextTick vs Microtasks vs setImmediate
topics.summary: The precise execution order of synchronous code, nextTick, promises, timers and setImmediate.
topics.description:
Several APIs let you "run this soon". Their order is a classic interview topic.

### The priority order
1. **Synchronous code** of the current script
2. **`process.nextTick` queue**
3. **Promise microtasks** (`.then`, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask`)
4. **Macrotasks** in event loop phases: timers, I/O callbacks, `setImmediate`

After each macrotask callback, Node drains nextTick first and then the microtask queue, and repeats until both are empty.

### Details
* `nextTick` is Node-specific and runs before promise callbacks (in CommonJS). In an **ES module** the top-level code itself runs as a microtask, so promise callbacks queued there run **before** nextTick callbacks. Inside later callbacks (timers, I/O) the CommonJS order applies.
* `setTimeout(fn, 0)` vs `setImmediate(fn)` in the main module is **not deterministic** (depends on process speed). Inside an I/O callback `setImmediate` always wins.
* `setImmediate` runs in the check phase after poll; `setTimeout` runs in the timers phase.

### Starvation
A recursive `process.nextTick` (or endless microtasks) never lets the loop move to I/O or timers, freezing the program. `setImmediate` recursion is safe because the loop runs between calls.

### Use cases
* `nextTick`: emit an event after the constructor returns, so listeners can attach
* `setImmediate`: yield to I/O in a long computation, split work into chunks
* `queueMicrotask`: schedule small follow-up work

### await and ordering
`await x` continues in a microtask, so code after `await` runs before any timer.
keyPoints: Order: sync, nextTick, promise microtasks, then timers/I/O/setImmediate
setTimeout 0 vs setImmediate is nondeterministic in the main module
Inside I/O callbacks setImmediate runs before timers
Recursive nextTick can starve I/O
ES module top-level code runs promise callbacks before nextTick
pitfalls: Relying on setTimeout 0 versus setImmediate order outside I/O

interview.q: Output order of nextTick, Promise.then and setTimeout?
interview.a: Synchronous code first, then nextTick callbacks, then promise callbacks (microtasks), then timers and other macrotasks. So nextTick runs before then, and then runs before setTimeout 0.

interview.q: Why can process.nextTick be dangerous?
interview.a: Its queue is drained completely before the event loop continues. If callbacks keep scheduling more nextTicks, I/O and timers never run (starvation).

topics.title: Streams: Readable, Writable, Transform
topics.summary: Process data in chunks instead of loading it all: the four stream types, modes and async iteration.
topics.description:
A **stream** processes data piece by piece, so you can handle files larger than memory and start sending output before all input has arrived. Streams are everywhere in Node: `fs`, `http` requests/responses, `net` sockets, `zlib`, `process.stdin/stdout`.

### Four kinds
| Type | Direction | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Readable** | source | `fs.createReadStream`, `http.IncomingMessage`, `process.stdin` |
| **Writable** | destination | `fs.createWriteStream`, `http.ServerResponse`, `process.stdout` |
| **Duplex** | both, independent | TCP socket |
| **Transform** | Duplex that modifies data | `zlib.createGzip()`, crypto ciphers |

### Reading from a Readable
* Async iterator (best): `for await (const chunk of readable) { ... }`
* Events: `'data'`, `'end'`, `'error'`, `'close'`
* `readable.pipe(writable)` (older) or `pipeline()` (preferred)

### Writing
`writable.write(chunk)` returns a boolean. `writable.end()` finishes the stream and fires `'finish'`.

### Chunk types
Chunks are `Buffer` (or strings with an encoding). With `objectMode: true` chunks can be any JS value, handy for parsing pipelines.

### Create your own
`new Transform({ transform(chunk, enc, cb) { cb(null, chunk.toString().toUpperCase()); } })` or with an async generator: `Readable.from(asyncGenerator())`.

### Web Streams
Node also implements the browser `ReadableStream` API (used by `fetch` bodies). Convert with `Readable.fromWeb` and `Readable.toWeb`.

### Why it matters
Copying a 4 GB file with `readFile` needs 4 GB of RAM. A stream needs roughly 64 KB at a time.

Four types: Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform
for await..of is the cleanest way to consume a Readable
Chunks are Buffers unless objectMode or encoding is set
Always handle the error event (or use pipeline)
pitfalls: Loading entire files with readFile when a stream would do
Forgetting an 'error' listener on a stream
Treating each 'data' chunk as a complete line or JSON document

interview.q: What are the four types of streams?
interview.a: Readable (data source), Writable (destination), Duplex (both ways, like a socket) and Transform (a duplex that changes data as it passes, like gzip).

interview.q: Why use streams instead of readFile?
interview.a: Streams process data in small chunks, so memory use stays constant for any file size and processing can start before the whole input is available, improving latency and scalability.

topics.title: Backpressure and pipeline
topics.summary: How streams slow a fast producer for a slow consumer, and why pipeline beats pipe for error handling.
topics.description:
If a source produces data faster than the destination can consume it (a fast disk and a slow network client), the extra data piles up in memory. **Backpressure** is the mechanism that tells the producer to pause.

### How it works
Every stream has an internal buffer limited by `highWaterMark` (16 KB default, 64 KB for fs streams, 16 objects in objectMode).
* `writable.write(chunk)` returns **`false`** when the buffer is full
* Stop writing and wait for the `'drain'` event
* `readable.pause()` and `resume()` control the flow on the reading side

Hand-written version:
`if (!res.write(chunk)) { readable.pause(); res.once('drain', () => readable.resume()); }`

### pipe handles it, but...
`readable.pipe(writable)` applies backpressure automatically but has weak error handling: if one stream errors, the others are **not destroyed** and file descriptors leak.

### Use pipeline
`stream.pipeline(a, b, c, cb)` or the promise version `await pipeline(a, b, c)` from `node:stream/promises`:
* Connects the streams with backpressure
* On any error, **destroys all** streams and reports the error once
* Resolves when the last stream finishes
* Accepts async generator functions in the middle as transforms

### Async generators as transforms
`await pipeline(source, async function* (chunks) { for await (const c of chunks) yield c.toString().toUpperCase(); }, destination)`

### Compose and finished
`stream.compose()` joins streams into a single duplex. `stream.finished()` (or `finished` promise) waits for a stream to end or fail.

### Diagnosing memory growth
If memory grows steadily while piping, someone is writing without respecting `drain` (for example a loop calling `write` hundreds of thousands of times).

highWaterMark sets the buffer size threshold
pipe() does not clean up on error; pipeline() does
Async generator functions can act as transforms inside pipeline
Ignoring backpressure is a classic memory leak
pitfalls: Ignoring the return value of write() in loops

interview.q: What is backpressure?
interview.a: A flow-control mechanism: when a consumer cannot keep up, write() returns false and the producer must pause until the 'drain' event, preventing unbounded memory use. pipe and pipeline handle it for you.

interview.q: Why prefer stream.pipeline over .pipe()?
interview.a: pipeline forwards errors from any stream, destroys all streams to avoid leaks and gives a single callback or promise for completion, whereas pipe leaves the other streams open when one fails.

topics.title: AbortController and Cancellation
topics.summary: Cancel fetch, timers, streams, child processes and your own async work with AbortSignal, including timeouts.
topics.description:
**`AbortController`** is the standard way to cancel asynchronous operations. The same API exists in browsers.

### Parts
* `const ac = new AbortController()`
* `ac.signal` is an `AbortSignal` you pass to cancellable APIs
* `ac.abort(reason?)` triggers cancellation; the signal's `aborted` becomes `true` and an `abort` event fires

### Who accepts a signal?
`fetch`, `fs.readFile` / `fs.watch` / `writeFile`, `timers/promises`, `child_process`, `events.once`, `stream.pipeline`, `http.request`, `readline`, `net`, `dns/promises`, and many libraries (axios, undici, database drivers).

### Handy helpers
* `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` aborts automatically after a delay (rejects with `TimeoutError`)
* `AbortSignal.any([s1, s2])` aborts when any signal aborts (user cancel **or** timeout)
* `signal.throwIfAborted()` checks inside your own loops

### Cancelled operations reject
They reject with an `AbortError` (`err.name === 'AbortError'`). Treat that as expected, not as a failure to log loudly.

### Make your own functions cancellable
Accept `{ signal }` as an option, check `signal.aborted` between steps, listen with `signal.addEventListener('abort', cleanup, { once: true })` and pass the signal on to the APIs you call.

### Use cases in servers
Cancel database queries and upstream requests when the client disconnects; enforce per-request timeouts; stop watchers and background loops during shutdown.

AbortSignal.timeout(ms) is a one-line timeout
AbortSignal.any combines multiple cancellation sources

Pass the signal down through your own functions

interview.q: How do you add a timeout to a fetch request?
interview.a: Pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) to fetch. If the time passes before the response, the promise rejects with a TimeoutError.

interview.q: Why accept an AbortSignal in your own async functions?
interview.a: It lets callers cancel the work (timeouts, user navigation, shutdown), frees resources early and integrates with the rest of Node's APIs.

topics.title: Error Handling in Async Code
topics.summary: Handle rejections, uncaught exceptions and operational errors correctly so one bug does not silently corrupt your server.
topics.description:
### Two kinds of errors
* **Operational errors**: expected runtime problems (network down, file missing, invalid input, DB timeout). Handle and respond.
* **Programmer errors**: bugs (`undefined is not a function`). Fix the code; the safest reaction is to log and restart.

### Rules for promises and async/await
1. Every promise chain ends with `.catch()` or sits inside `try/catch` with `await`.
2. Return or await promises; a "floating" promise's error becomes an `unhandledRejection`.
3. Throw `Error` objects (they have stack traces), never strings. Use `new Error('msg', { cause: err })` to keep the original error.
4. In a `Promise.all` all other promises keep running even though the first rejection settles the result.

### Global safety nets (last resort)
`process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` and `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)`. After an uncaught exception the process state is unknown. **Log and exit**, and let a process manager (PM2, Docker, Kubernetes) restart it. Do not keep running.

### Callbacks and event emitters
Errors in callbacks are passed as the first argument. Emitters need an `'error'` listener. `try/catch` around them does nothing.

### Custom error classes
Create `class AppError extends Error { constructor(msg, status) { super(msg); this.status = status; } }` so you can map errors to HTTP status codes in a central handler.

### Express
Express 5 forwards rejected promises from async handlers to the error middleware automatically. In Express 4 you must wrap handlers or call `next(err)`.

### Never swallow errors
An empty `catch {}` hides bugs. Log at least and decide: retry, return a friendly error or rethrow.

Always catch awaited promises or end chains with catch
Throw Error objects and use the cause option
After uncaughtException: log and exit, let a supervisor restart
Custom error classes make HTTP mapping easy

Continuing after an uncaughtException

interview.q: What is the difference between operational and programmer errors?
interview.a: Operational errors come from the environment (timeouts, bad input, missing file) and can be handled gracefully. Programmer errors are bugs in the code; the process state may be inconsistent, so you log and restart.

interview.q: What should you do in an uncaughtException handler?
interview.a: Log the error, close resources if possible and exit with a non-zero code. Rely on a supervisor (PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes) to restart; continuing can leave the app in a corrupt state.

topics.title: Not Blocking the Event Loop
topics.summary: Recognise CPU-heavy synchronous code that freezes your server and break it up, offload it or stream it.
topics.description:
One slow synchronous task freezes **every connected client**, because there is only one JavaScript thread. A healthy Node service keeps each callback short (a few milliseconds).

### Typical blockers
* Sync APIs in handlers: `readFileSync`, `execSync`, `pbkdf2Sync`, `zlib.gzipSync`
* Big loops, sorting millions of items, heavy recursion
* `JSON.parse` / `JSON.stringify` on very large payloads
* **ReDoS**: a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking on user input
* Large `Buffer` and string operations, `replace` on huge text

### Symptoms
High latency for all routes, health checks timing out, timers firing late, CPU at 100% on one core. Measure with `monitorEventLoopDelay` or `clinic doctor`.

### Strategies
| Strategy | How |
|---|---|
| Partition | Process in chunks and yield with `await setImmediate()` between chunks |
| Offload | `worker_threads` pool (piscina), or another service |
| Stream | Parse big payloads incrementally (stream-json, ndjson) |
| Use async APIs | `fs.promises`, `crypto.pbkdf2` (thread pool) |
| Limit input | Max body size, safe regexes (`safe-regex`, RE2) |
| Queue | Move heavy jobs to a background worker (BullMQ) |

### Fairness trick
`import { setImmediate as yieldLoop } from 'node:timers/promises'` then `await yieldLoop()` every N iterations lets pending I/O run.

### Rule of thumb
If a task takes more than about 50 ms of pure CPU, do not run it directly on the request path.

ReDoS and big JSON parsing are common hidden blockers

interview.q: How do you find out that the event loop is blocked?
interview.a: Watch event loop delay or utilisation (perf_hooks), look for slow responses across all routes and profile with --cpu-prof or clinic. Timers firing much later than scheduled are a symptom.

interview.q: What is ReDoS?
interview.a: Regular expression Denial of Service: a pattern with nested or ambiguous quantifiers takes exponential time on crafted input, blocking the single thread. Avoid such patterns, limit input size or use a safe engine like RE2.

topics.title: Graceful Shutdown
topics.summary: Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT by stopping new connections, finishing in-flight work and closing resources before exiting.
topics.description:
When you deploy, scale down or press Ctrl+C, the operating system or orchestrator sends a signal. If you just die, in-flight requests get cut, database transactions are lost and queues can be left half processed. **Graceful shutdown** means finishing cleanly.

### Steps
1. Listen for `SIGTERM` (Docker, Kubernetes, PM2, systemd) and `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C).
2. Mark the app as **not ready** (health check returns 503) so load balancers stop sending traffic.
3. Stop accepting new connections: `server.close()` (waits for existing ones to end).
4. Finish or abort in-flight work; use a **deadline** (for example 10 seconds).
5. Close databases, Redis, queues, file handles.
6. Exit with code `0`; if the deadline passes, force exit with code `1`.

### Keep-alive connections
`server.close()` waits for idle keep-alive sockets. Use `server.closeIdleConnections()` and `server.closeAllConnections()` (Node 18.2+) or set a timer to force close.

### Kubernetes details
Default grace period is 30 seconds between SIGTERM and SIGKILL. Add a small `preStop` sleep so the endpoint is removed from the load balancer first. Docker: use `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` (exec form) so Node is PID 1 and receives the signal; `npm start` often swallows signals.

### Run shutdown once
Guard with a flag, because a user can press Ctrl+C twice or two signals can arrive.

### Test it
Start the server, send a long request, then `kill -TERM <pid>` and verify it still completes.

examples.title: Shutdown handler
examples.explanation: A request in progress when you press Ctrl+C still receives "done" before the server exits.

interview.q: Why implement graceful shutdown?
interview.a: To avoid dropping in-flight requests and corrupting data during deploys or scaling: stop accepting new work, finish current work, close connections and then exit.

interview.q: Why might SIGTERM not reach a Node app in Docker?
interview.a: If the container runs npm start or a shell script as PID 1, that wrapper may not forward signals. Use the exec form CMD ["node", "server.js"] (or tini / --init) so Node itself receives the signal.
